title: ElasticMM: Efficient Multimodal LLMs Serving with Elastic Multimodal Paral

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract versus Introduction, Section 4.2, and Conclusion
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract claims that ElasticMM reduces TTFT by up to 6.8× and achieves 5.1–7.2× higher throughput. The Introduction instead claims up to 4.2× TTFT reduction and 3.2×–4.5× throughput, and Section 4.2/Conclusion repeat the latter figures. No experiment in the paper reports the abstract's 6.8× or 5.1–7.2× numbers. These are materially inconsistent headline results and require correction or supporting results.

predicted_errors.error_location: Figure 6 table, Qwen-2.5-VL column at SLO scale 1.0
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The displayed values state approximately 250 QPM for vLLM and approximately 450 QPM for DistServe at SLO 1.0, while labeling the DistServe result as '(4.5×)'. Based on the displayed values, 450/250 = 1.8×, not 4.5×. The numerical multiplier is inconsistent with the plotted/tabulated quantities.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.1 Metrics and Section 4.2 Input Latency
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper defines normalized input latency as 'average prefill time divided by input length,' then describes this quantity as 'i.e., time-to-first-token (TTFT).' TTFT is ordinarily elapsed time from request arrival to the first emitted token and includes queueing and, for multimodal requests, preprocessing and image encoding. Dividing prefill time by token count is neither TTFT nor even measured in the same units. Therefore claims of TTFT reduction cannot be inferred from this defined metric without separately reporting end-to-end TTFT.

The baselines are said to use 'default settings' but also to be 'extended to support multimodal inference as needed.' Those are materially non-default modifications, especially for DistServe, whose cited design is prefill/decode disaggregation for LLMs rather than a specified multimodal serving implementation. The paper does not describe the modifications, stage placement, caching behavior, parallelism, batching settings, or validation of the extensions. This prevents reproduction and makes the baseline comparison uninterpretable as a comparison to the cited systems.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.1 Model and Dataset; Section 4.3 ablations
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The evaluation says it uses Poisson arrivals and 'real-world production service traces' but neither identifies the traces nor gives their modality mix, arrival distribution, prompt/output length distributions, image counts/resolutions, trace duration, warm-up, sampling procedure, or cache state. The ablation further uses an unspecified 'mixed dataset composed of two distinct sources.' These omitted workload and cache-hit details are central to claimed gains from elasticity and prefix caching and make the reported performance results non-reproducible.

The paper states that the two-model evaluation demonstrates 'universal applicability across all MLLM architectures, including cross-attention, prefix-tuning, and adapter-based models.' Only Qwen2.5-VL-7B and LLaMA3.2-Vision-11B are evaluated. No prefix-tuned or adapter-based model is named, configured, or tested. The universal compatibility conclusion exceeds the presented evidence.

The manuscript repeatedly makes absolute claims unsupported by its evaluation, including that EMP 'completely eliminates all inference bottlenecks,' that the design 'eliminates resource contention and maximizes utilization,' and that it guarantees SLO compliance 'under all workload conditions.' The experiments use one eight-GPU single-node machine, two models, two datasets, and selected synthetic/unspecified traces. They cannot establish elimination of all bottlenecks, maximization, or compliance under all workloads.

The prose defines burst tolerance as 'the difference between peak load and idle capacity normalized by total instances,' but Equation (1) defines bt(i) as the ratio N_i^peak/N_i^avg. A difference and a ratio are not equivalent. Moreover, N_i^peak and N_i^avg are described as numbers of instances a group 'can use' for peak/average load, rather than quantities defined as functions of the allocation being greedily changed. Thus the stated greedy allocation objective is not mathematically specified by the equation.

The appendix describes data parallelism as partitioning one input i into i_1,...,i_n, computing g_E^j(i_j), and gathering the results. That is not data parallelism: data parallelism replicates the model and assigns independent examples/requests to replicas; partitioning a single input requires a model-, sequence-, or spatial-parallel algorithm with model-specific communication. Therefore Equation (13) does not justify the claimed invariance of a request's result under changing data-parallel degree.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix B.4/B.8, claims of exact parallelism invariance and numerical stability
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The proof asserts that deterministic CUDA operations and fixed-order reductions make results identical 'regardless of partition count.' Changing a parallelism configuration changes reduction grouping, kernel selection, and often floating-point operation order; determinism only makes a given configuration repeatable, not equal to every other configuration. The stated fp16 error scale of approximately 10^-7 is also inconsistent with fp16 precision (whose unit roundoff is on the order of 10^-4 to 10^-3, not 10^-7). Hence the claimed exact-output theorem and the argument that argmax changes are 'statistically negligible' are not established.

The appendix reports 100% bit-identical outputs and average token-probability differences below 10^-8 across 1,000 prompts, but provides no decoding parameters, precision mode, deterministic-kernel configuration, parallelism configurations, migration events, cache-hit cases, hardware settings, seed, or raw results. These details are indispensable for evaluating the exceptional bit-identity claim, particularly because the preceding proof incorrectly assumes invariance across changed parallel configurations.

predicted_errors.error_location: References [21] and all citations of [21] as the LLaMA 3.2 Vision model
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Reference [21] is titled 'Llama Guard 3 Vision: Safeguarding human-AI image understanding conversations.' It is not the Llama 3.2 Vision model reference cited in Table 1 and Section 4.1. Using a safety-model paper as the source for Llama 3.2 Vision architecture/model claims is a misattribution.

predicted_errors.error_location: References [29] and all citations of [29] as Qwen2.5-VL
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Reference [29] is explicitly titled 'Qwen2-VL: Enhancing vision-language model's perception of the world at any resolution,' whereas the paper evaluates and discusses Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-72B. Qwen2-VL and Qwen2.5-VL are distinct releases; the cited reference does not substantiate model-specific Qwen2.5-VL claims.

The text states 'Zhang et al. [61] proposed a similar two-tier separation in 2024,' but the bibliography ends at reference [60]. Reference [61] is absent, so the claimed prior work cannot be identified or checked.

The text attributes 'Flash-Decoding' to citation [55]. Reference [55], however, is Tri Dao's 'FlashAttention-2: Faster attention with better parallelism and work partitioning.' This is a different work and does not support the stated Flash-Decoding attribution.

The sentence 'Further implementation details are provided in Appendix 6' points to an appendix/section that does not exist. The supplied appendices are Appendix A and Appendix B, and neither is numbered Appendix 6.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix B title, Theorem 1, and Appendix B.10 conclusion
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The appendix claims a formal guarantee of 'exact inference equivalence' and concludes that ElasticMM yields 'the exact same inference results.' The proof obtains this only by assuming lossless state transfer, deterministic identical execution across hardware and parallelism settings, exact cached values, and unchanged computation; several of those assumptions are precisely what must be demonstrated and one is invalid for changed parallel configurations. The theorem is therefore circular/conditional rather than a proof of the claimed system-wide exact equivalence.
